title: Sum of Minimums Over All Slices
statement:
You get an array of positive integers nums. Look at every contiguous, non-empty slice of it and take that slice's smallest value. Return the sum of all those minimums.

The sum can be huge, so return it modulo 1 000 000 007. Slices are counted by position: two slices with the same values at different places both count.

examples.why: The ten slices have minimums 3, 1, 2, 4 (single values), 1, 1, 2 (pairs), 1, 1 (triples) and 1 (all four). They add up to 17.
Slices [2], [2] and [2, 2], each with minimum 2. With equal values, be careful to count the slice [2, 2] once, not once for each 2.
One slice, and its minimum is 5.

hints: Instead of looping over slices, flip it around: for each element, in how many slices is it the minimum?
Element i is the minimum of every slice that starts after the nearest smaller element on its left and ends before the nearest smaller element on its right. That is (i − left) · (right − i) slices.
Find those nearest smaller elements with a monotonic stack. To avoid counting a slice twice when values repeat, use 'strictly smaller' on one side and 'smaller or equal' on the other.

explain.intuition:
There are about n²/2 slices, too many to visit one by one. Turn the question around: how much does each element contribute? Element i adds nums[i] once for every slice where it is the minimum. Those slices can stretch left until just before the nearest smaller element on the left, and right until just before the nearest smaller element on the right. If those are at L and R, there are i − L choices for the start and R − i for the end, so the contribution is nums[i] · (i − L) · (R − i).

Nearest smaller elements are what a monotonic stack finds in O(n). One subtlety: with equal values, like [2, 2], the slice [2, 2] has two candidates for its minimum. Make the rule asymmetric, stopping at "strictly smaller" on the left and at "smaller or equal" on the right, and every slice is credited to exactly one element: the rightmost copy of its minimum.
steps: For each i, find L[i]: the index of the nearest element to the left that is strictly smaller, or −1.
For each i, find R[i]: the index of the nearest element to the right that is smaller or equal, or n.
Both come from one stack pass: when nums[i] pops an index j (because nums[j] ≥ nums[i]), set R[j] = i. After popping, the top of the stack is L[i].
Add nums[i] · (i − L[i]) · (R[i] − i) to the answer, modulo 1 000 000 007.
pitfalls: Using 'strictly smaller' on both sides. With repeated values, slices like [2, 2] are counted twice.
Using 'smaller or equal' on both sides. Then such slices are counted zero times.
Overflow: the product can exceed 32-bit range. In JavaScript it stays below 2⁵³ here, but take the modulo after each addition.

solutions.title: Every start, running minimum
solutions.idea: Fix the start of the slice and extend it to the right, keeping the running minimum and adding it at every step.

solutions.title: Contribution with a monotonic stack
solutions.idea: Each element is the minimum of (i − L) · (R − i) slices, where L and R are its nearest smaller neighbours. One stack pass finds both.

followups: Return the sum of (maximum − minimum) over all slices.
Solve it with a DP: if you know the sum of minimums of slices ending at i − 1, how do you get the one for slices ending at i?
